*Mutti*German{}|Etymology}Derived from t1mother.|Pronunciation}/ˈmʊti/}Ⓓ0/00/De-@^.ogg|Noun}(fem.,plural:[s.gen][@^s][s][-only with an article])}#mom,mummy|Usage notes}The word is commonly used with a definite article in most parts of central Germany,southern Germany,and Austria:''Wo ist die @^?'' – “Where is Mum?” In northern Germany—and generally in writing—no article tends to be used:''Wo ist @^?''}The genitive ''@^s'' is used before the modified term,without any article or determiner:''@^s Tasche'' – “Mum’s bag”. This is chiefly northern German usage; the rest of the language prefers:''die Tasche von der @^'' (as above). — With an accompanying article or determiner,the genitive takes no ending:''die Tasche meiner @^'' – “my mum’s bag”. This,however,is not common usage in any region; children will say instead:''die Tasche von meiner @^''.|Derived terms}Eislaufmutti|Proper noun}(fem.)}#''a nickname for'' Angela Merkel}•synononym:[Mama],[Angie]

*Nacht*German{}|Etymology}From Middle High German naht,from Old High German naht,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆naht,from Proto-Germanic ⋆nahts,ultimately from Proto-Indo-European ⋆nókʷts. Akin to from Dutch nacht,from English night,from Danish nat,from Gothic 𐌽𐌰𐌷𐍄𐍃.|Pronunciation}/naxt/+naχt+naxt}Ⓓ/5/51/De-@^.ogg(Germany)(Germany)}Ⓓ/6/64/De-@^2.ogg(Germany)(Germany)}LL-Q188 (deu)-Sebastian Wallroth-@^.wav(Germany)}Ⓓ/2/2b/De-at-@^.ogg(Austria)(Austria)|Noun}(fem.,plural:[Nächte],diminituve:[Nächtchen])}#night}•Die '''@^''' war lang und frostig.}•The night was long and chilly.}#darkness}•Sie wurden von der '''@^''' verschlungen.}•They were engulfed by the darkness (of the night).|Usage notes}In contemporary German,''@^'' is used somewhat differently than cog:night. Although ''@^'' can be a general term for the dark hours of the day,when used as a time measurement it refers only to those hours when most ordinary people are in bed (roughly 11 p.m. till 6 a.m.). So while one says in English:“Let's have a beer tonight!”,in German one needs to say:''Lass uns heute'' Abend ''ein Bier trinken!'' (“Let's have a beer this evening!”)}In English,one says ''in the night'' or ''in the day'' referring to a time of day,but ''on that night'' or ''on that day'' referring to a date. German,instead,always uses in with  and always uses an with Tag (except when the latter simply means “time,era”,e.g. ).}A (masculine) genitive @^s occurs only in the phrases des @^s and eines @^s and alone as the adverbial genitive @^s (cp. nachts).|Derived terms}col-auto:Gebnacht|See also}list:times of day/de||Low German{}|Etymology}From from Middle Low German nacht,from from Old Saxon naht,from from Proto-West Germanic ⋆naht,from from Proto-Germanic night,from from Proto-Indo-European night.|Pronunciation}/ˈnaxt/|Noun}#night||Pennsylvania German{}|Etymology}From Middle High German nacht,from Old High German naht,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆naht,from Proto-Germanic ⋆nahts,ultimately from Proto-Indo-European ⋆nókʷts. Compare from German @^,from Dutch nacht,from English night.|Noun}#night

*Nachzeitigkeit*German{}|Etymology}From nach-+Zeit+-ig+-keit.|Noun}(fem.)}#grammar post-timeliness; succedent|Usage notes}In grammar,describes the relationship of different grammatical tenses in main and subordinate clauses,in which the action of the subordinate clause takes place after that of the main clause. For instance,in the sentence "''Bevor der Arzt einen Patienten untersucht,desinfiziert er seine Hände.''" ("Before the doctor examines a patient,he disinfects his hands."),the word bevor is used to create the post-timeliness:The subordinate clause ("the doctor examines a patient") takes place after that of the main clause ("he disinfects his hands").|Coordinate terms}Gleichzeitigkeit,Vorzeitigkeit

*Nehrung*German{}|Etymology}From East Prussian from Middle High German tspit,related with the adjective from Proto-Germanic ⋆narwaz,whence from English narrow. If from Middle High German nerge is an early contraction,the word may have been derived with the Germanic suffix from Proto-Germanic ⋆-ingaz commonly used in placenames (compare from German -ingen). If,however,the form  (16th c.) is a later alteration of from Middle High German nerge,it could be an old ablaut form or derived with the Germanic suffix from Proto-Germanic ⋆-į̄ (then orginally meaning “narrowness”).|Pronunciation}/ˈneːʁʊŋ/}Ⓓb/bf/De-@^.ogg}Ⓓ/e/e4/De-at-@^.ogg(Austria)(Austria)}Neh+rung|Noun}(fem.)}#geography spit Literally:[long,very narrow peninsula,especially in the Baltic Sea]}•Frische '''@^'''}•Vistula spit}•Kurische '''@^'''}•Curonian spit|See also}Haff

*Netzteil*German{}|Pronunciation}Ⓓ0/0b/De-@^.ogg|Noun}(mask.,genitive:@^s,plural:[@^e])}#power supply}#}• Schaltnetzteile sind ein weit verbreitetes Betriebsmittel zur Wandlung der netzseitigen Wechselspannung in Gleichspannung. In IT-Systemen werden vorwiegend solche Schaltnetzteile zur Versorgung der internen Systemkomponenten verbaut. Ohne spezielle Filter stellen diese '''@^e''' den einzigen Schutz für die interne Hardware gegenüber leitungsgeführten Störsignalen dar. Im Allgemeinen stellen Schaltnetzteile aber durch den notwendigen Transformator und die hochfrequenten Schaltvorgängen selber eine elektromagnetische (EM) Störquelle da. Daher wird die elektromagnetische Störaussendung speziell in der Norm EN 50950 und der EMV-Richtlinie 2004/108/EC geregelt. Die Norm weder die Richtlinie schreiben nähere Untersuchung einer Schutz- wirkung gegenüber bewusst hervorgerufenen leitungsgeführten Störungen vor.

*niemand*German{}|Alternative forms}Niemand|Etymology}From Middle High German nieman,from Old High German nioman; equivalent to nie+Mann. Cognate with from Hunsrik nimmand.|Pronunciation}/ˈniːmant/}Ⓓc/c1/De-@^.ogg|Pronoun}#nobody,no one}•synononym:keiner}•Antonym:jemand}•Es ist gar '''@^''' da.}•There's '''no one''' at all.}#}• Den Tod '''@^''' zwingen kunnt.|Usage notes}''Niemand'' is synonymous with keiner,which is the nominalised masculine form of the pronoun kein. In written German,''@^'' is more common than ''keiner'',whereas colloquial German often prefers the latter. (Note that ''keiner'' can also be used in other senses,in which ''@^'' is not applicable.)}''Niemand'' may or may not take the case endings ''-em'' (dative) and ''-en'' (accusative). Thus:“''Ich suche @^''” and “''Ich suche @^'''en'''''” are both correct translations of “I'm looking for nobody.” The latter is somewhat more common (at least in writing). Using ''@^en'' in the dative is incorrect,but it's a common error and occurs with surprising frequency in print. It was possible historically,but not in Modern German.}With a following adjective,''@^'' is always uninflected. The adjective itself is capitalized and declined in the strong pattern. It generally uses neuter forms:''@^ Neu'''es''''' – "nobody new". In the accusative case it may also take a masculine form:“''Ich suche @^ Neu'''en'''''” alongside “''Ich suche @^ Neues.''” ("I'm looking for nobody new.") The dative form has ''-em'' either way. The genitive case cannot be used with an adjective,but needs to be paraphrased.|Derived terms}Niemand}Niemandsland

*nimmer*German{}|Etymology}Perhaps originally ni+immer,thus the same construct as from English ever and from English never. According to others a dialectal contraction of nie mehr,later remodelled according to immer.|Pronunciation}/ˈnɪmər/+-mɐ}/ˈnimɐ/,(Austria)Bavaria}Ⓓ6/66/De-@^.ogg|Adverb}#regional no more,no longer}•Liegt der Bauer tot im Zimmer,lebt er '''@^'''.}•If the farmer lies dead in his room,he's alive '''no more'''.}•qjoke in the form of a Bauernregel}#regional never again}#archaic never,at no time}#}• Meiner Mutter Haar ward '''@^''' weiß. ('''Never''' did my mother's hair become white.)|Usage notes}In northern Germany and many parts of central Germany,the word is used mainly in some set phrases such as nie und @^. Otherwise,it sounds archaic or poetic. It is used more readily in southern Germany and Austria,meaning “no more” or “never again”. The original sense “never,at no time” is now rare.|Synonyms}sense:no more nicht mehr}sense:never again nie mehr,nie wieder}sense:never nie,niemals|Derived terms}@^mehr}Nimmersatt

*nur Bahnhof verstehen*German{}|Etymology}Earlier 20th century. Literally:[to understand only train station].}According to some sources (e.g. Duden) from WWI military slang. For front soldiers,Bahnhof would have been synonymous with furlough or relocation to the hinterland,so the phrase would originally have meant “to understand only what one wants to hear”,“not to pay attention”. What may corroborate this theory is the variant .}Other suggested origins:}Train stations are noisy,hectic places with whirring engines,shouting passengers,unintelligible announcements etc.}The word  (and its equivalents in other languages) would typically have been familiar to international travellers even if they knew hardly any other word of the local language.|Pronunciation}/nuːɐ̯ ˈbaːnhoːf fɐˈʃteːən/}Ⓓ7/7c/De-@_.ogg|Verb}#idiomatic to understand nothing at all}#idiomatic to deliberately not pay attention to a conversation

*Nutte*German{}|Alternative forms}censored|Etymology}Originally meant young girl,young prostitute in the dialect of Berlin. Further origin unsettled. Possibly from Middle Low German not,from Middle Low German nut in the sense of vulva,vagina (compare Cognate German Nuss,which has this sense in hunter's jargon); or from Nut,also in the aforementioned sense,but less probably,since this word is not Low German. An alternative hypothesis considers it a variation of lütt from Middle Low German small,possibly through a merger with menstruating woman,but the vocalism ''-u-'' does not really agree with this. Finally,since the connection with prostitution is apparently very old,a relation with from Middle Low German useful,profitable might be considered.|Pronunciation}/ˈnʊtə/}Ⓓ/a/a2/De-at-@^.ogg(Austria)(Austria)}Rhymes:ʊtə|Noun}(fem.)}#informal whore; prostitute}•synononym:Thesaurus:Prostituierte}#}• Und draußen vor der großen Stadt/Stehen die '''@^n''' sich die Füße platt|Derived terms}nuttig}@^nbrause}@^nköfferchen

*nutzen*German{}|Alternative forms}overall less common,but usage varies by sense and region; see lemma|Etymology}From Middle High German @^,from Middle High German nützen,from Old High German nuzzōn,from Old High German -nuzzen (in from Old High German ginuzzen),from Proto-Germanic ⋆nutōną,from Proto-Germanic ⋆nutjōną,from Proto-Germanic ⋆nutjaną. Compare modern Nutzen.}The verb is originally restricted chiefly to Upper German and East Central German,the former preferring the form ''@^'',the latter preferring ''nützen''. By way of hypercorrection,''nützen'' has now become a chiefly southern form. Low German and West Central German originally use other verbs,namely,brauchen for the transitive and batten for the intransitive function. These areas prefer ''@^'' in modern standard German.|Pronunciation}/ˈnʊtsən/+ˈnʊtsən+ˈnʊtsn̩}Ⓓ5/5e/De-@^.ogg}nut+zen|Verb}#transitive to make use of; to deploy; to exploit; to harness; to take (the opportunity of)}•synononym:[Gebrauch machen von],[wahrnehmen]}•Du solltest deine Talente '''@^'''.}•You should '''make use''' of your talents.}•Wenn sich ihnen so eine Gelegenheit bietet,dann '''@^''' sie die.}•When such an opportunity offers itself to them,they’ll '''take''' it.}#transitive to be useful,to be of use,to do good}•Er hört mit der Diät auf,weil sie nichts '''nutzt'''.}•He's stopping the diet because it '''is''' no '''use'''.}•Was '''nutzt''' es schon,sich anzustrengen?}•What '''is the use''' of making an effort anyway?}#transitive to benefit,to help,to do good to @^ ( with  acc/datsomeone)}•Er hat sich überall angebiedert,aber das hat ihm auch nicht '''genutzt'''.}•He curried favour with everybody,but that didn’t '''help''' him either.|Usage notes}There is a distinction between ''@^'' and be@^. The former is used with opportunities or options,the latter is used with means or instruments. Sometimes this is just a matter of aspect. For example,“He uses the computer” can be phrased as ''Er benutzt den Computer'' (mere mechanical sense),or ''Er nutzt den Computer'' (implying that the computer is,in whatever way,an opportunity).|Synonyms}sense:be useful; benefit helfen; etwas bringen qualifier:colloquial|Antonyms}antsense:be useful; benefit schaden|Derived terms}ab@^}aus@^}be@^}Nutz}Nutzen}Nutzer}nützlich

*oberer*German{}|Etymology}From Old High German obaro.|Pronunciation}/ˈoːbəʁɐ/}Ⓓe/e1/De-@^.ogg|Adjective}#upper}•Mein Portmonee ist in der '''oberen''' Schublade.}•My purse is in the '''upper''' drawer.}#superior|Usage notes}Since the adjective is already semantically comparative in its positive form,the grammatical comparative forms are very rare and heard in the vernacular only. They might be used to mean “even more above”. For example:''Mein Portmonee ist in der oberen Schublade.'' − ''In dieser?'' − ''Nein,in der noch '''@^en'''.'' (“My purse is in the upper drawer.” – “This one?” − “No the one above that.”)}The superlative forms are perfectly normal,being the same as cog:uppermost. When referring to a hierarchy,"chief" or "head" may be better translations,for example Oberster Richter}•Chief Justice.|Derived terms}Ober|See also}über}oben

*Omi*German{}|Etymology}Diminutive form of Oma.|Pronunciation}/ˈoːmi/}Ⓓ2/23/De-&_.ogg|Noun}(fem.,plural:[s.gen][sprenominal without an article])}#grandma,granny,nan|Usage notes}The word is commonly used with a definite article in most parts of central Germany,southern Germany,and Austria:''Wo ist die &_?'' – “Where is Grandma?” In northern Germany—and generally in writing—no article tends to be used:''Wo ist &_?''}The genitive ''&_s'' is used before the modified term,without any article or determiner:''&_s Tasche'' – “Grandma’s bag”. This is chiefly northern German usage; the rest of the language prefers:''die Tasche von der &_'' (as above). — With an accompanying article or determiner,the genitive takes no ending:''die Tasche meiner &_'' – “my grandma’s bag”. This,however,is not common usage in any region; children will say instead:''die Tasche von meiner &_.''|Coordinate terms}Opi

*Opi*German{}|Etymology}Diminutive form of Opa.|Pronunciation}/ˈoːpi/}Ⓓ0/07/De-&_.ogg}Ⓓ4/42/De-&_2.ogg|Noun}(mask.,plural:[&_s],diminituve:[&_lein])}#grandpa|Usage notes}The word is commonly used with a definite article in most parts of central Germany,southern Germany,and Austria:''Wo ist der &_?'' – "Where is Grandpa?" In northern Germany—and generally in writing—no article tends to be used:''Wo ist &_?''}The genitive ''&_s'' is used before the modified term,without any article or determiner:''&_s Tasche'' – “Grandpa’s bag”. This is chiefly northern German usage; the rest of the language prefers:''die Tasche vom &_'' (as above). — The genitive can also be used with an accompanying article or determiner:''die Tasche meines &_s'' – “my grandpa’s bag”. This,however,is not common usage in any region; children will say instead:''die Tasche von meinem &_.''|Coordinate terms}Omi

*orange*German{}|Etymology}From the noun Orange,from fr.|Pronunciation}/oˈʁãːʃ/,/oˈʁaŋʃ/,/oˈʁɔ̃ːʃ/,/oˈʁɔŋʃ/,(predicative only)}/oˈʁãːʒə/,/oˈʁaŋʒə/,/oˈʁɔ̃ːʒə/,/oˈʁɔŋʒə/,(non-predicative feminine and plural forms)}Ⓓ0/0e/De-@^.ogg|Adjective}#@^|Usage notes}The adjective has two sets of forms. In the formal standard language,endings are added directly to the stem (''orang-''). In less formal style and in the vernacular,another set of forms is used in free variation,in which an ''-n-'' is infixed before the endings.}It is also officially correct to leave the adjective entirely undeclined. This usage is rare,however,and seems dated.

*Orlog*German{}|Alternative forms}obsolete|Etymology}As a High German word from Middle High German urliuge,from Middle High German urlouge,from Middle High German twar,from a merger of from Old High German urliugi and from Old High German urlag,respectively from Proto-Germanic twar and from Proto-Germanic tdestiny. The word had become almost obsolete by the 16th century and was then continued only through reinforcement by cognate from Middle Low German ōrloch,from Middle Low German ōrlōge,from Middle Low German ōrlāge. The main form subsequently became ,finally ,the latter being likely influenced also by from Dutch oorlog. Originally the same word as from German notext1 colubrid,which see.}The form is based on the common dialectal development ''-ā-'' → ''-ō-'' with subsequent irregular shortening. Loss of initial ''n-'' is a common development in the Germanic languages and is due to metanalysis,i.e. the unetymological segmentation of preceding endings or articles,for example:''}eine notter'',dialectally ''}en notter'' → ''}en‿otter''. The same happened in from Dutch adder and from English adder. *Paar*German{}|Etymology}From Middle High German par,from Old High German par,from Latin pār.|Pronunciation}/paːr/+pʰaː(ɐ̯)+pʰaːʁ+pʰaːr}Ⓓ/4/47/De-at-@^.ogg(Austria)(Austria)}Ⓓ3/3f/De-@^.ogg}Rhymes:aːɐ̯|Noun}(neut.,plural:[@^(e)s],diminituve:[Päärchen])}#pair,couple}•Ein '''@^''' brauner Schuhe.}•A '''pair''' of brown shoes.}#twosome|Usage notes}''@^'' with capital 'P' always refers to exactly 2 items. ''Ein paar'' is also used more loosely,spelled with small 'p',to mean "a few". *paar*German{}|Pronunciation}/paːr/+paːɐ̯+paː+paːʁ}Ⓓ0/06/De-@^.ogg}Rhymes:aːɐ̯aː|Etymology 1}From Paar.|Determiner}#some; few; a few|Usage notes}This determiner can be preceded by a definite article and some other determiners:''Die @^ Tage sind ja schnell vorbei.'' (“These few days will be over soon.”) Otherwise,in standard German,''@^'' always takes the undeclined numeral ein in front of it:''Nach ein @^ Tagen ist das vorbei.'' (“After a few days it will be over.”) In colloquial German the numeral may be left out.}Although literally meaning “pair,couple”,the word does not commonly refer to two items,but rather to sets from three upward. The upper limit is dependent both on absolute number and percentage:10 out of 20 may be ''ein @^'',as may 50 out of 1,000; whereas 50 out of 100 are unlikely to be identified so.|Derived terms}Paarhufer}@^mal}Paarzeher|Adjective}#bar

*Pappe*German{}|Etymology}From Middle High German ⋆pappe (attested 15th century,but earlier the derivative from Middle High German pepelen,from the source of modern Papp.}Also compare modern päppeln. The original sense of the word was “pap,mush cooked from flour” and “wheatpaste,flour-based glue”. It was then used for a material of book covers made by gluing together several sheets of paper,whence finally “any thick layer of paper” (18th century). The older sense is continued by regional Papp,which see for more.|Pronunciation}/ˈpapə/}/ˈpɑpːə/,(Swiss)}Ⓓb/b8/De-@^.ogg}Rhymes:apə|Noun}(fem.)}#paperboard,cardboard}•synononym:Karton}#slang blotter acid Literally:[a piece of paper laced with LSD]}•synononym:Acid}#alternative form of [(Papp),tpap,( porridge; wheatpaste)]|Usage notes}The distinction between  and Karton is chiefly regional,the latter being preferred in the south,especially in Austria and Switzerland. (In the north,is used mainly as a countable noun meaning “cardboard box”.) In technical contexts and idiolectally,fine distinctions may be made between both words,but these vary and have little bearing on general usage.|Hyponyms}Dachpappe}Wellpappe|Derived terms}päppeln,pappen,pappig|See also}Pampe

*Park*German{}|Etymology}A doublet of inherited Pferch. The form ''@^'' was first borrowed in the 15th/16th centuries from Middle Dutch park,in which the word had developed the sense “recreation park,enclosed hunting grounds” under the influence of from Old French parc. German ''@^'' remained sporadic,however,until it was reinforced (or borrowed anew) from modern from French parc and English park from the late 17th century on. For the further origin of all mentioned cognates compare Pferch and from English park.|Pronunciation}/paʁk/+pʰaʁk+pʰaɐ̯k standard}/paːk/common; chiefly northern and central Germany}Ⓓ0/02/De-@^.ogg|Noun}(mask.,genitive:@^ses,plural:[Pärks][s][eless common][^erare outside Switzerland])}#park Literally:[piece of ground in or near a city or town,enclosed and kept for ornament and recreation]}#}@^ Auch die Vegetation des '''@^es''' war hier,wie allerwärts in Irland,eine bewundernswerthe.}•The vegetation of the '''park''',too,was here,as everywhere in Ireland,admirable.}#}• Aber oftmals lief die kleine Dorothee … noch viel weiter  bis dorthin  wo der regelmäßige Garten sich in einen weiten natürlichen '''@^''' verlor und allmählich in Wiesen und Wald überging. *patronym.*German{}|Adjective}#Abbreviation of [@-1isch]}#}'''1926–8''',Leumann–Hofmann–Szantyr,''Lateinische Grammatik'' I:''Lateinische Laut- und Formenlehre'' (2nd ed.,1977),<span style"font-variant:small-caps">Formenlehre Nomen</span> II.B,§ 273:1.d,:}#}:Das Hauptzeugnis für gr. lang+grc+-ειος,der aeol. Gebrauch von '''@^''' lang:-ειος bei ''o''-Stämmen,ist eine Neuerung; dieses lang:-ειος ist als Universalsuffix auch bei Kons.-Stämmen verwendet; und es stammt als ''-ios''-Ableitung von den Namen auf lang:-ης,so lang:-ειος neben lang:-ης in Thessalien,''Schwyzer'',Del. 567 (lang:-ης als lang:-εις geschrieben) l. 80 f. lang:Ἱπποκράτειος,99 f. lang:Ἀντιφάνειος,112 lang:Ἀντιγένειος; auf Lesbos '''@^''' 623,56 lang:Ἱερογένειος,640 lang:Σωγένειος,weibl. 621,11 als Name lang:Ἑλλανοκράτεια; das Muster für mask. lang:-γένειος usw. war vermutlich nicht-'''@^''' fem. lang:-εια (hom. lang:ἠριγένεια,lang:Ἰφιγένεια,lang:Εὐρύκλεια oder lang:-κλέεια).|The main evidence for Greek lang:-ειος,the Aeolic use of '''@-1ic''' lang:-ειος with ''o''-stems,is an innovation; this lang:-ειος is used as a universal suffix with consonant stems; and it derives from nouns in lang:-ης as a ''-ios''-derivation,thus lang:-ειος is near lang:-ης in Thessaly,''Schwyzer'',Del. 567 (lang:-ης written as lang:-εις) vid. 80 f. lang:Ἱπποκράτειος,99 f. lang:Ἀντιφάνειος,112 lang:Ἀντιγένειος; '''@-1ic''' on Lesbos 623,56 lang:Ἱερογένειος,640 lang:Σωγένειος,fem. 621,11 as the name lang:Ἑλλανοκράτεια; the example for the masculine lang:-γένειος etc. was presumably the non-'''@-1ic''' fem. lang:-εια (Homeric lang:ἠριγένεια,lang:Ἰφιγένεια,lang:Εὐρύκλεια or lang:-κλέεια).

*Pech*German{}|Etymology}From Middle High German pech,from Middle High German bech,from Old High German peh,from Old High German beh,from Proto-West Germanic tpitch,tar,wood resin.}The form is unusual as it shows unshifted ''p-'',but shifted ''-ch'',even though the shift of initial ''p-'' to ''pf-'' occurred later than that of postvocalic ''-k'' to ''-ch''. Theodor Frings therefore considered that the word was at first restricted to West Central German along the Rhine (which lacks the ''pf''-shift) and only spread to Upper German slightly later when the shift was no longer active. *Pflock*German{}|Etymology}From Middle High German pfloc (late 14th century). Related with from Middle Low German plügge (1375,or from Middle Low German plugge),also from Middle Low German pluck,from Middle Low German plock (ca. 1420),from Dutch plug (1511 as from Dutch plugghe,also from Dutch plogge),all “peg,wooden nail,pin,plug." Probably from the same ultimate source as from English plug.}Further origin uncertain. The word shows semantic relations with a nominal derivative of from Proto-Germanic ⋆plukkijaną (“to pluck”,from Middle High German phlucke,phlocke,from Middle Low German pluck,from Dutch plok),and at least in High German also with the descendant of from Proto-Germanic tblock. However,these relations are in all likelihood secondary. Within High German,the word appears to have been restricted chiefly to the north-east (East Central German and surroundings); therefore it has been argued to be a Low German borrowing in the colonial regions,but the late attestations in all languages make it hard to prove this. from English plug and similar Scandinavian forms are usually considered borrowings.|Pronunciation}/pflɔk/,(standard)}/flɔk/,(northern and central Germany)}Ⓓe/e9/De-@^.ogg}Vlog|Noun}(mask.,genitive:@^es,plural:[@^e])}#stake or wooden peg used to fasten something}•synononym:Pfahl|Derived terms}Zeltpflock
